sentences: In the 1970s big city, the heir, the son of a powerful real estate tycoon the tycoon, marries the young woman, a working-class student.
Together they try to establish a new life in a rural state, setting up a health food store called by an optimistic name.
However, the tycoon manipulates the heir into returning to the city, telling him that the young woman deserves more than he's currently giving her.
Upon their return, the young woman brings up the idea of having children.
The heir says it will never ever happen, which leads the young woman to assume something is wrong with his fertility.
After buying a lake house, the young woman confesses to their pregnant neighbor that she is expecting as well.
The heir responds angrily upon finding out and forces the young woman to make an appointment for an abortion.
He misses the appointment when he is called away to do work for his father.
The young woman enters medical school while her relationship with the heir continues to deteriorate.
She makes inquiries about a separation, but her funds, which she needs in order to pay for school, are cut off when she attempts to leave.
Having been advised that she will need leverage to compel the family to give her a settlement, the young woman attempts to find incriminating documents of their financial activities.
She then disappears without a trace in 1982, despite a $15,000 reward offered for any information on her whereabouts.

Eighteen years later, the case is reopened by the district attorney after reading an unpublished novel written by the heir's best friend, the confidante, which contains a murder almost identical to the family's case.
Soon after this is announced, the confidante is shot and killed in her home, and the heir is under suspicion again while standing trial for the murder of his neighbor the victim in another state.
The heir is acquitted of the murder of the victim; the film states that nobody has ever been tried for the confidante's murder and that the young woman remains a missing person to this day.
A flash-back implies that the heir left his wife's remains in the trunk of her car, which the father finds.
The film ends with the heir visiting his dying father and whispering to him, "I miss her so much."
It's left to the viewer to decide whether he is talking about the young woman or his mother.
The caseworker is a social worker assigned to investigate the family of the 10-year-old girl, as her grades have declined and an emotional rift with her parents has emerged.
The caseworker suspects that the parents have been abusing and overprotecting the girl since the day she was born, and proposes to her department to take the child away from her parents' custody.
Eventually, the caseworker's suspicions are confirmed when the girl's parents try to kill her by roasting her alive in their oven.
The caseworker saves the girl with the help of the detective.
The girl is to be sent to a children's home, but she begs the caseworker to look after her instead.
With the board's agreement, the caseworker is assigned to care for the girl until a suitable foster family is found.
In the meantime, the girl's parents are placed in a mental institution since they are no longer fit for their parental responsibility for the girl, according to the court.
After the girl moves in, strange things begin to happen around the caseworker.
Another of the caseworker's cases, a young boy, murders his parents, and the detective informs the caseworker that somebody phoned the boy from her house the night before the crime.
As she is suspected of involvement in the incident, the girl undergoes a psychiatric evaluation by the caseworker's best friend, the psychologist.
During the session, the girl turns the evaluation around, asking the psychologist what his fears are and subtly threatening him.
That night, after receiving a "strange phone call" at his apartment, the psychologist is panicked by the sight of a mass of hornets coming out of his body.
His panic causes him to fall and break his neck on the toilet, killing him instantly.
The caseworker becomes suspicious about having the girl in her home, so she heads to the mental asylum to seek answers from the girl's parents.
They tell her that the girl is a demon who feeds on feelings, and that they tried to kill her in an attempt to save themselves and others.
The girl's father tells the caseworker that the only way to kill the girl is to get her to sleep.
Shortly after the caseworker leaves the asylum, both parents die: her mother is fatally burned, and her father is stabbed in the eye with a fork.

The detective thinks the caseworker should seek psychiatric help, but is later convinced when he receives a similar strange phone call in his home from the caseworker's cellphone, which is being used by the girl.

He arms himself at the police precinct to aid the caseworker in handling the girl; however, he inadvertently and fatally shoots himself in the head with a shotgun when the girl makes him imagine he is being attacked by permanently ferocious dogs.

After realizing that her closest colleagues have been eliminated, and that the rest of her cases will be next, that night, the caseworker has the girl drink tea spiked with sedative, and while the girl is asleep, the caseworker sets fire to her house, hoping and attempting to get rid of her.
However, the girl escapes unharmed.
The police offer to escort the caseworker and the girl to a temporary place to stay.
As the caseworker follows the police cars, she suddenly takes a different route and drives at high speed, hoping to instill fear in the girl.
She then drives the car off a pier.
As the car sinks, the caseworker struggles to lock the girl (now in her true demon form) in the trunk.
The caseworker then exits the car, but as she swims away, the surviving girl grabs her leg after punching a hole through the car's taillight, in an attempt to prevent her escape.

The caseworker struggles to break free until the caseworker overcomes her strengths and fears, which causes the girl to finally let go of the caseworker as the car continues to sink, finally defeating the girl from the inside.
As the caseworker climbs back ashore, she is relieved to be rid of the girl, hence bringing the case itself to a close.
Criminal defense attorney the lawyer works in a big-city county, in a western state, from the back of his black luxury sedan, chauffeured by the driver.
He typically works for low-end criminals including the gang leader, leader of a biker gang.
His ex-wife, the prosecutor, with whom he shares a daughter, is a district attorney who disapproves of his choice of clientele.
The lawyer is unexpectedly hired to represent the client, a wealthy rich-suburb playboy and the son of real estate mogul the matriarch.
The client is accused of viciously beating prostitute the accuser, and surprisingly chose the lawyer specifically for the case.
The lawyer and his investigator, the private eye, analyze photos and evidence and find similarities to a prior case where a prostitute was killed.

The lawyer represented the defendant, the convict, and due to the overwhelming evidence and in spite of the convict's earnest proclamations of innocence, convinced him to plead guilty to avoid the death penalty.
The lawyer visits the convict, who becomes agitated when he shows him the client's photo.
The lawyer realizes that the client is likely the killer.
His own hands tied, the lawyer tells the private eye to investigate the client.
When he gets back home, he sees that someone broke into his house.
He stumbles upon the client, who learned that the lawyer visited the prison earlier.

The client nonchalantly admits to committing the murder for which the convict was convicted and says he chose the lawyer as counsel in order to bind the lawyer by attorney–client confidentiality rules and keep him from talking about either case.
He also makes veiled threats towards the lawyer's daughter.
Later, the private eye is found shot dead after leaving him a voicemail message claiming he found the convict's "ticket out of jail."
The lawyer learns that the bullet that killed the private eye matches his late father's antique.22 pistol, which is missing from its box; this means the client framed the lawyer for the killing.
During the trial, the lawyer ruthlessly cross-examines the accuser and discredits her.
He also secretly sets up a known prison informant, the snitch, to testify against the client with furnished information on the previous murder.
The lawyer is able to discredit the snitch's testimony, getting the client's current charges dismissed.
However, when the client is set free, the police arrest him immediately for the previous attack based on the snitch's description.
The driver gives the lawyer a gun, acting on the lawyer's earlier request.
The client's family gets him released due to lack of evidence and he goes to the prosecutor's home, where the lawyer is waiting, having monitored the tracking device still attached to the client.

The lawyer vows that he will not stop until the convict is freed and the client is convicted for his crime AND for killing the private eye; the client mockingly tells him he cannot guard his family all the time; but the biker gang arrives on cue and bashes the client's luxury vehicle before beating him badly enough to send him to the hospital.
The prosecutor discovers the private eye had found a parking ticket issued to the client near the murder victim's house, strong evidence against him.
Upon arriving home, the lawyer is surprised by the client's mother, who had broken in.
When the lawyer tells her he is going to get her son convicted of the private eye's murder, she says "My son didn't kill him, I did" and shoots the lawyer with the pistol.
Hit in the midsection, the lawyer falls back and before the matriarch can fire again, he pulls his gun and kills her.
In the epilogue we learn that the convict has been released and the DA is seeking the death penalty for the client.

As the lawyer and the driver drive off, he is pulled over by the gang leader and the biker gang, whose case he takes pro bono in gratitude for their help, though he reminds the driver he will charge more for later cases.
The railroad executive pilots an airplane in pursuit of another plane.
The railroad executive asks herself, "Who is the mystery man?" before apparently crashing into a mountainside.
Nine months earlier, the railroad executive is trying to understand the abandoned prototype of an advanced motor she and her lover the industrialist have found.

Scientists across the country have been disappearing under mysterious circumstances, but the railroad executive is able to locate the scientist, who agrees to help from an abandoned laboratory in a western state.

The railroad executive's brother the company president, president of the family railroad company, meets store clerk the shopgirl and brings her to see a renowned pianist, who disappears during his performance, leaving a note asking, "Who is the mystery man?"

Later, at the company president and the shopgirl's wedding, the railroad executive's friend the mine owner argues with other guests about whether money is evil, and secretly informs the industrialist about devastating explosions at his copper mine—the next day.
The industrialist spends the night with the railroad executive.
Later, he is confronted about the affair by his wife the socialite, but when he offers a divorce she declines, in order to maintain her position in society.

The industrialist sells his advanced alloy to the coal magnate's coal mining company, but refuses to sell it to the federal government, in defiance of the newly enacted "sharing" law that forces businesses to sell to all buyers.
The two are charged under the law.
The railroad executive barges into the coal magnate's office, realizes that he too is about to disappear, and understands that she is close to understanding the force behind the disappearances.
At trial, the industrialist defends individual freedom and the pursuit of profit, and is given only a token penalty by the court, which fears turning him into a martyr.
The government announces "the directive", which freezes employment and production and requires that all patents be gifted to the government.
The industrialist defies this decree as well, but relents when he is blackmailed with photos of himself and the railroad executive that would damage the railroad executive's reputation.
When the railroad executive hears about the industrialist's "gift" and her brother's complicity, she quits the railroad.

During her absence, a family railroad train collides with a military train in a tunnel, due largely to political pressure by a passenger and human error by the railroad executive's poorly trained replacement.
This impels the railroad executive back to her job.
The mine owner tries to dissuade her from returning, as he had earlier tried to talk the industrialist into leaving his business, but she returns anyway.
The railroad executive takes a train to a mountain state to show her faith in the railway, but its engine fails.
The repair technician used to work for a motor company, which produced the motor the railroad executive found.
He tells the railroad executive how the need-based reward system in his company failed, and his coworker the mystery man left the company vowing to "stop the motor of the world".
The railroad executive calls the scientist, who tells her that he is quitting.
The railroad executive buys a small airplane and flies to the western state to try to dissuade him, but as she is landing, she sees him get into a plane on the airstrip.
After a pursuit in the air—the opening scene of the film—the railroad executive's plane crashes in a valley hidden by stealth technology.
A wounded railroad executive crawls to the edge of her crashed plane, where she is greeted by the mystery man.
The film ends with a quote from the author: "Money is the barometer of a society's virtue.
But when you see that in order to produce it, you need to obtain permission from those who produce nothing...
You will know that your society is doomed.
The nurse lives in a small town in a northwestern state called the settlement.
She is the town's local nurse, widowed by her husband, who was the town's doctor.
The settlement was formerly a prosperous mining town, but has become poverty-stricken.
There is little work, the school has been closed and the town has virtually vanished from the map.
During her day, the nurse visits several families.
The teenager and the sister live with their mother and her violent, alcoholic boyfriend, who has impregnated the sister.
Despite this, their mother did not kick him out, drawing the nurse's ire.
Instead, she sends away the sister and her baby, whom the nurse helped to deliver.
Because of her rough life, the teenager is selectively mute, communicating through a journal she carries.
She also sketches things she's seen, including "the phantom".
This is a local legend or urban myth surrounding a being who abducts local children who are never seen again.
The nurse returns to her large home on the outskirts of the settlement, which she shares with her son the little boy and his nanny.
She eats dinner, puts the little boy to bed, and falls asleep on a couch.
She awakes to a noise downstairs, followed by a loud radio sermon.
She finds the nanny bound and gagged, then rushes to her son's bedroom, finding him gone.
While in pursuit of what the viewer believes is "the phantom", it is gradually revealed that the little boy is not her son at all, but rather one of the kidnapped children.
The kidnapper is actually the real mother of the boy, attempting to take back her child.
The rest of the town, skeptical of the mother's accusations, agree to give her a chance to prove her claims.
The nurse, with the help of the teenager, pursues the mother, reacquires the little boy, and hands him off to "the phantom" in the tunnels which run under the town, left over from the defunct mine.
The teenager begs her to send the phantom to take her, too.
The nurse initially refuses but then relents, cautioning her to remain silent about it until the phantom comes for her.
The nurse then waits in her house.
The police and federal agents arrive, as does an angry mob.
The nanny hangs herself, and the nurse is taken to jail, where she is despised and threatened as a child killer.
The nurse admits to kidnapping and murdering the children, but the confession is later revealed to be a lie.
Soon after, the teenager watches her mother engage in a drunken fight with her boyfriend, before laughing with him over it.
Disgusted, the teenager walks off into a nearby field, where she finds the phantom waiting for her—the nurse's husband, who is not dead after all.
He takes her to an empty house in a nearby city, providing her with new clothes.
He then delivers her to a new family, with a new identity.

The phantom refuses payment, saying that the organization faces massive risks to rescue each child, with the nurse martyring herself to save the organisation, which "rescues" young children from bad homes and places them with good ones, in an attempt to break the cycle of poverty and abuse which passes from one generation to the next.
In the settlement, the teenager's birth mother grieves over her runaway daughter, the town continues to decline, and the nurse sits in prison.
The police have given up on finding the children, thinking that the nurse buried them in the tunnels which run for miles and are dangerous to traverse because of cave ins, etc.
In comparison, the teenager lives in a beautiful home, where her art is encouraged, and she has the best of everything.
She has begun to talk and seems well-adjusted and happy.

As she walks to an art class, she gives a voice-over expressing love and gratitude toward her three mothers: her birth mother, whom she misses; the nurse, who gave her a chance at a new life; and her new mother, who is providing her with everything she could ever want.
As she crosses a park, she sees the little boy with his new family, which he now accepts as his own.
(The teenager thinks he and the other younger ones have forgotten and do not recognize her, but the visual cues leave it decidedly open-ended).
Despite getting her wish of a better life, she sometimes wishes to return.
The teenager's closing thoughts question society's implication that her new life is better.
Five married men share ownership of an upmarket loft, which they use for discreetly meeting their respective mistresses.
When the body of a murdered woman the victim is found in that loft, the men begin to suspect each other of having committed the gruesome crime, as they are the only ones with keys to the premises.
Through flashbacks, which are intertwined with scenes from the present, the story is unravelled.
The five men are: the architect: architect and designer of the building where the loft is situated.
Married to the architect's wife and father of their children, he initially suggests the five friends use the loft as a private oasis.
He is set up by the other men to be accused of the murder.
The psychiatrist: a psychiatrist married to the psychiatrist's wife and the elder maternal half-brother to siblings the half-brother and the younger sister.
He is the most reluctant of the men to the loft idea and the last to accept a key; the psychiatrist eventually does so because he is attracted to the escort, who eventually becomes his mistress.
The escort warns the psychiatrist not to fall in love with her because she is a prostitute, and he gives her his key as proof he does not use the loft with other women.
The third friend: married to the third friend's wife, who is an insulin-dependent diabetic.
He discovers the body in the loft and initially calls the architect and the others over.
The police later insinuate that the third friend is attracted to the architect, and it is the third friend who records the men's activities in the loft without their knowledge.
The drinker: heavy drinker and a conspicuous lecher.
He and his wife the drinker's spouse separate when a woman the drinker slept with on a business trip shows up at their house.
The half-brother: half-brother to the psychiatrist and recently married to the heiress, the only daughter of a wealthy property developer who is also the half-brother’s boss.
The half-brother is a drug user who grew up in a dysfunctional household with his abusive father and is very protective of his younger sister the younger sister.
He warns the other men off from having sex with her.
At the 1964 international exposition, young inventor the inventor attempts to showcase his homemade jet pack, but it fails and does not impress the judges.
However, a mysterious girl, the recruiter, sees potential in him.

She gives him a lapel pin marked with a “T” and directs him onto the entertainment company's boat ride, where the pin triggers a hidden transport to the secret city—a dazzling futuristic city in another dimension.
There, robots repair his jet pack, allowing him to soar through the city and join its secret community of innovators.
In the present, teenage optimist the dreamer continually sabotages the demolition of a space agency launch platform in hopes of saving her father’s job.
After she is arrested, she discovers a secret city pin among her belongings.
Touching it transports her to the futuristic world, but only as a projection; when the pin’s power is expended, she abruptly returns to her normal reality.
Determined to understand what she saw, the dreamer follows clues to a memorabilia shop in a southern city, where the owners attack her for information about the pin.
The recruiter bursts in and defeats the owners, actually animatronic robots, who self-destruct, blowing apart the shop.
After the dreamer and the recruiter steal a car, the recruiter reveals she is also an animatronic, purposed to find and recruit people who fit the ideals of the secret city.
The recruiter brings the dreamer to a now-adult inventor, who is a bitter recluse living in the northern part of the state.
Banished from the secret city years earlier, the inventor wants nothing to do with the place.
The dreamer discovers he has built a device predicting the imminent end of the world, but her refusal to accept that future causes the probability to drop—something the inventor has never seen.
When robotic assassins arrive to eliminate them, the inventor reluctantly joins the dreamer and the recruiter.
Using a teleportation device, they travel to a European capital and launch an old rocket hidden beneath the famous tower.

The inventor explains that the secret city was created by the founding group, a secret society of visionaries lead by an engineer, a novelist, a physicist, and an industrialist, who sought a place free from political and commercial interference.
Arriving in the secret city, the trio finds the once‑utopian city in decline.
The governor greets them and leads them to a tachyon machine the inventor invented which can view possible futures.
It has been broadcasting visions of global catastrophe to the home planet.
The dreamer realizes the machine’s warnings have become a self-fulfilling prophecy: humanity, overwhelmed by doom, simply stopped trying to prevent disaster.
The governor admits he intended the images as a wake‑up call, but when the world ignored them, he gave up and decided to let the apocalypse unfold.
The dreamer, the inventor, and the recruiter attempt to destroy the machine, but the governor fights to stop them.
During the struggle, the recruiter foresees the governor killing the inventor.
She sacrifices herself to save him by triggering her self‑destruct sequence.
The explosion destroys the tachyon device, and the falling wreckage kills the governor.
In the aftermath, the dreamer and the inventor take leadership of the secret city.
They recruit the dreamer’s father and brother, and they build a new generation of recruiter‑like animatronics.
Given secret city pins, these childlike robots set out across the world to find new dreamers, thinkers, and inventors—people capable of building a better future.
A contagious disease ravages the planet.
The father, the mother and their teenage son the teenager live a secluded lifestyle in their home, deep in the woods in an undisclosed location.
After the mother's father the grandfather contracts the disease, they euthanise him and burn his body.
That night, they capture an intruder breaking in.
The father ties him to a tree and places a bag over his head, leaving him there overnight to confirm he is not suffering from the disease.
The stranger, the newcomer, explains he was searching for fresh water for his wife and young son.
The newcomer offers to trade some food for water.
The mother suggests taking the strangers in, on the reasoning that with more people it would be easier to defend themselves.
The father reluctantly agrees and drives the newcomer to collect his family.
Along the way, they are ambushed by two men.
The father kills them, while accusing the newcomer of setting him up.
The newcomer assuages the father's mistrust.
The father returns with the newcomer, his wife the newcomer's wife, and son the little boy.

After establishing their rules, which include keeping the only entrance locked with a key the father or the mother wear around their neck, the two families establish a sense of normality and grow closer.
One day, the teenager's dog the pet begins barking aggressively at an unseen presence and chases it into the woods.
The teenager, who had followed the pet, insists he heard something in the woods.
That night, the newcomer seemingly contradicts a story he told the father earlier, resulting in the father's increasing distrust of the newcomer.
That evening, the teenager discovers the little boy sleeping on the floor of the grandfather's old room, suffering from a nightmare.
He also finds the front door of the house open.
The families investigate, finding a bleeding and gravely sick pet on the floor.
They euthanise and burn the dog.
After the teenager reveals the door was open, the mother suggests that a sleepwalking little boy opened the door, causing more distrust.
The father suspects the little boy is infected, and decides they should quarantine in their separate rooms to ensure no one is sick.
That evening, the teenager is awakened by a nightmare about his grandfather.
The next morning, the teenager overhears the little boy crying constantly and the newcomer's wife telling the newcomer they need to leave.
The teenager informs his parents that he too may be infected.
The father and the mother don protective masks and gloves, and take weapons to confront the newcomer's wife and the newcomer.
The newcomer draws a gun and takes the father captive.
He insists his family is healthy, repeatedly tells the little boy to keep his eyes shut and orders the father to remove the mask.
The newcomer demands the father give him a "fair share" of food and water so they can leave.
The mother and the father overwhelm the newcomer, and force him and his family outside.
The newcomer tries to beat the father to death until the mother shoots the newcomer, killing him.
The newcomer's wife flees into the woods with the little boy.
The father fires at them, killing the little boy, then the newcomer's wife.
Later, the teenager awakens in bed, visibly sick.
His mother comforts him as he dies.
The father and the mother, now visibly infected, sit at the dinner table in silence.
They share a shattered, devastated look.
In the city of 2049, bioengineered humans known as replicants are still used for slave labor.

The officer (short for serial number, a serial code), a latest-model replicant, works for the city police department as a "blade runner", an officer who hunts and "retires" (kills) rogue replicant models.
After "retiring" replicant the farmer, the officer finds a box buried under a tree at the farmer's farm.
It contained the remains of a female replicant who died during a caesarean section.
This demonstrates that replicants could reproduce biologically, previously thought impossible.
The officer's superior, the lieutenant, fears this knowledge will lead to war between humans and replicants, so she orders the officer to retire the replicant child and destroy all related evidence.
The officer visits the CEO's corporation, successor to the defunct earlier corporation in the manufacture of replicants.
DNA archives identify the deceased female as an experimental earlier-model replicant.
The officer learns of her romantic ties with former blade runner the veteran.
The CEO wants the secret to replicant reproduction to expand interstellar colonization.
He sends his replicant enforcer, the henchwoman, to monitor the officer.
An unidentified figure engages several prostitutes in the city, including one named the streetwalker, to keep eyes on the officer.
At the farmer's farm, the officer finds the date 6.10.21 carved into the tree trunk and recognizes it from a childhood memory of a wooden toy horse.
Because replicant memories are artificial, the officer's holographic AI girlfriend the companion suggests that this is evidence that the officer was born, not created.

The officer discovers in police department records that two children born on that date have identical DNA, but are inexplicably registered as being opposite genders, and that the girl died from a genetic disorder.
The officer's search for the boy leads him to an orphanage, but the records from the year in question are missing.
The officer recognizes the orphanage from his memories and finds the toy horse in the furnace where he remembers hiding it.

He then visits replicant-memory-maker the scientist, who confirms that his memory of the orphanage is a real memory that someone lived, leading the officer to conclude he is the deceased replicant woman's son.
The officer then fails a baseline test, marking him as rogue.
When he implies to the lieutenant that he killed the replicant child, she gives him 48 hours to pass the test, or he will be retired himself.
The companion hires prostitute replicant the streetwalker to sync with to be able to have sex with the officer.
The following morning, the streetwalker places a tracker in the officer's jacket prior to leaving.
The officer then takes the wooden toy horse to be analyzed for its origin, which leads him to the ruins of a now radioactive desert city.
There he finds the veteran, who informs him that the deceased replicant woman was named the beloved, and that he is the father of the beloved's child.
The veteran had helped the replicant resistance scramble the birth records to protect the child's identity.
The veteran then left the child with the resistance to ensure the hunted child would not be found through him.
The henchwoman, who has killed the lieutenant, tracks the officer to the desert city.
She kidnaps the veteran, destroys the companion, and leaves an injured officer behind.
Using the streetwalker's tracker, the resistance rescues the officer.
Their leader, the rebel commander, reveals that the beloved's child was actually a girl.
Fearing that the veteran may give up the freedom movement to the CEO and endanger the child, the rebel commander urges the officer to kill him.
The officer deduces that the memory of the toy horse actually belongs to the scientist, who is the beloved's daughter.
The henchwoman takes the veteran to meet the CEO, who offers the veteran a duplicate beloved in exchange for information about the child's whereabouts.
The veteran refuses the offer, so the CEO has the henchwoman kill the duplicate.
As the henchwoman transports the veteran to be tortured off-world, the officer intercedes.
He fights and drowns the henchwoman but is mortally wounded in the process.
The officer tells the veteran that he will be presumed dead, and is now free to go to his daughter, and then takes him to the scientist's facility.
Standing outside the facility, he hands the veteran the toy horse.
The veteran enters the building and meets the scientist, while the officer dies on the front steps.
After a night of drunken partying, the student wakes up on her birthday in the dorm room of classmate the young man.
She dismisses him and returns to her room.
Her sorority housemate the roommate surprises her with a cupcake for her birthday, which she throws away rudely.
The student meets with her married professor, the lecturer, with whom she is having an affair, almost being caught by the lecturer's wife.
That night, on her way to a party, the student is lured into a tunnel and murdered by a figure wearing a mask.
She immediately wakes up back in the young man's bed and is unnerved to find the previous day's events repeating themselves.
Baffled, she relives the day, this time avoiding the tunnel and reaching the party.
However, the masked killer follows her and murders her again.
The student again wakes up in the young man's bed, realizes she is in a time loop, and barricades herself in her room to avoid death.
The killer, already hiding inside, murders her a third time.
Waking up, the student explains the events to the young man.
He suggests taking advantage of the loop to identify her killer.
She spends the next several iterations trailing suspects but she is killed each time.
After waking from a loop where she is bludgeoned, the student faints and awakens in the campus hospital.
When the killer shows up, she escapes the hospital in the lecturer's car, only to be pursued and killed again.
Back in the young man's bed, the student convinces him of her predicament by demonstrating her knowledge of the day's events.
She sees a news report on the prisoner, a serial killer being held at the campus hospital.
Concluding that the prisoner is her killer, she rushes to the hospital to warn of his escape.
The prisoner breaks free and nearly kills the student, but the young man follows and rescues her.
The prisoner kills the young man before chasing the student to a bell tower, where she manages to subdue him with a crowbar.
Before delivering a fatal blow, she realizes that if she kills the prisoner and ends the loop, the young man will remain dead forever.
Therefore, she runs to the top of the tower and hangs herself from the bell rope.
The student awakens in the young man's dorm room and finds him alive again.
Now confident in solving her murder, she proceeds happily through the day.
She apologizes and offers friendship to the roommate, ends her affair with the lecturer, and meets her estranged father for lunch, where they begin to reconcile.
That night, she goes to the hospital and traps and kills the prisoner.
Relieved to be free, she celebrates her birthday in the young man's room and finally eats the cupcake the roommate gave her.
The next day, the student wakes up still in the loop.
Horrified, she returns to her room with the intent to run away, when the roommate offers her the cupcake again.
The student realizes that the previous loop was the only time she ate the cupcake, and she had died in her sleep; this meant that the roommate had poisoned the cupcake.
The roommate is her true killer, and when the student threw away the poisoned cupcake, the roommate used her job as a nurse to frame the prisoner for the student's murder.
The roommate admits to also having an affair with the lecturer, whose preference for the student drove her insane with jealousy.
She then attacks the student, but the student manages to stuff the poisoned cupcake in her mouth, then kicks her out of a second-floor window to her death.
At a restaurant, the student and the young man muse over the day's events, and he offers her his room for the night.
The next day, she wakes up believing she is still in the time loop, but the young man quickly reveals he was just playing a prank on her and it is really the next day.
The student is too relieved to be angry at him, and the two kiss.
